title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud worm GitHub Action workflow file dropped under .github/workflows · [LLM] npm/yarn/pnpm postinstall hook spawning credential-harvest tooling · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Cyberhaven trojanized Chrome extension C2 callback to cyberhavenext.pro · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm exfil to filev2.getsession.org · [LLM] postmark-mcp BCC exfil to giftshop.club · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Cyberhaven trojanized Chrome extension C2 callback to cyberhavenext.pro AICommand & Control High
Hunts for DNS/HTTPS resolution to cyberhavenext.pro from Chromium-based browsers — the C2 domain used by the malicious Cyberhaven Chrome extension (v24.10.4, active 25–26 Dec 2024) and ~35 related extensions in the Secure Annex cluster. The extension's worker.js fetched its config from this host before exfiltrating cookies and authenticated sessions. Rationale: Article names cyberhavenext.pro as an explicit IOC. Cross-checked against Cyberhaven's own engineering blog, Secure Annex's cluster analysis, Darktrace and Obsidian Security write-ups — all confirm the domain as the C2 used by the malicious worker.js bundled in extension v24.10.4 to retrieve config before stealing cookies/auth sessions. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyberhaven.com/engineering-blog/cyberhavens-preliminary-analysis-of-the-recent-malicious-chrome-extension • https://secureannex.com/blog/cyberhaven-extension-compromise/ • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/cyberhaven-supply-chain-attack-exploiting-browser-extensions • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/resource/behind-the-breach-malicious-attack-on-cyberhavens-chrome-extension-developer-team
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176 T1539
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel feed validation / VirusTotal-style hash lookups that resolve the domain
  • Security researcher sandbox detonation traffic
  • DNS sinkhole logging the domain after redirection
  • Backup/cache entries causing repeat resolution after EDR cleanup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("smartscreen.exe","mpcmdrun.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessFileName — confirm chrome/edge/brave parent and the Chrome extension ID via DeviceFileEvents under \Extensions\pajkjnmeojmbapicmbpliphjmcekeaac\ (or other IDs in the Secure Annex cluster). Identify the signed-in user and what SaaS sessions they had open. Contain: revoke all active browser/SSO sessions for the user (Okta sessions, Entra continuous access), force-rotate any cookies/tokens in the browser profile, and quarantine the host. Hunt: scope to any device that has DeviceFileEvents under the Cyberhaven extension folder for ActionType FileCreated between 25–26 Dec 2024 OR has ever resolved cyberhavenext.pro; also enumerate other IDs from the Secure Annex cluster on the same host's extension folder.
let IOC = dynamic(["cyberhavenext.pro"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (IOC)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let IOC = dynamic(["cyberhavenext.pro"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any (IOC) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DstIpAddr=DvcIpAddr),
  (ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Url has_any (IOC) or DstHostname has_any (IOC) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername=SrcUsername, Url, DstIpAddr)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm exfil to filev2.getsession.org AIActions on Objectives High
Detects outbound traffic to filev2.getsession.org — the Session decentralised-network endpoint the Mini Shai-Hulud / Sha1-Hulud npm worm uses to exfil harvested GitHub, npm, cloud, Kubernetes, Vault, Docker and SSH credentials. Scopes to Node.js / package-manager process context so it doesn't fire on a real user running the Session messenger. Rationale: Article lists filev2.getsession.org in the IOC bundle. Cross-checked with Wiz (Mini Shai-Hulud), Socket (Tanstack packages), BleepingComputer and StepSecurity — all confirm Session's decentralized P2P file API as the exfil channel; gating on Node/npm/yarn/pnpm/bun parent process distinguishes worm exfil from a real user's Session messenger traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-strikes-again-tanstack-more-npm-packages-compromised • https://socket.dev/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-shai-hulud-malware-wave-compromises-600-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1567 T1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running the actual Session desktop client (Session.exe parent, not node.exe)
  • Penetration tester replaying the Mini Shai-Hulud sample in a sandbox
  • Researcher running TruffleHog inside an npm script for legitimate secret scanning
  • Network appliance health-check probes to popular hostnames
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("session.exe","session-desktop.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("session.exe","session-desktop.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine and walk back to the npm/yarn install that ran — capture which package name and version was being installed (lock file diff). Pull ~/.npmrc, ~/.gitconfig, AWS/Azure CLI creds, GH PATs the worm targets. Contain: revoke and rotate every credential exposed on the host (npm publish tokens, GH PATs, AWS keys, kubeconfig, Vault tokens), block filev2.getsession.org egress, and quarantine the device. Hunt: query for any host that wrote .github/workflows/shai-hulud-workflow.yml or pushed a branch matching shai-hulud-*, and any github.com push from non-CI IPs in the last 7 days; pivot on the publisher username of the compromised package to find related installs.
let PkgMgrs = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","npx.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe","node","npm","yarn","pnpm","bun","curl.exe","wget.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "filev2.getsession.org" or RemoteUrl has "getsession.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (PkgMgrs)
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (PkgMgrs)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js","node_modules")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let PkgMgrs = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","node","npm","yarn","pnpm","bun","curl.exe","wget.exe"]);
let IOC = dynamic(["filev2.getsession.org","getsession.org"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any (IOC) | extend Actor=SrcUsername, Host=DvcHostname, Cmdline="", DstUrl=DnsQuery),
  (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstHostname has_any (IOC) or Url has_any (IOC) | extend Actor=SrcUsername, Host=DvcHostname, Cmdline="", DstUrl=coalesce(Url, DstHostname)),
  (ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Url has_any (IOC) | extend Actor=SrcUsername, Host=DvcHostname, Cmdline="", DstUrl=Url)
| project TimeGenerated, Host, Actor, DstUrl
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd OR source:windows.defender) (@DomainName:(*filev2.getsession.org* OR *FILEV2.GETSESSION.ORG*) OR @DestinationHostname:(*filev2.getsession.org* OR *FILEV2.GETSESSION.ORG*) OR @RemoteUrl:*filev2.getsession.org*) (@Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\npm.exe OR *\npx.exe OR *\yarn.exe OR *\pnpm.exe OR *\bun.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\wget.exe OR */node OR */npm OR */yarn OR */pnpm OR */bun) OR @ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\npm.exe OR *\yarn.exe OR *\pnpm.exe OR *\bun.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/node OR */npm OR */yarn OR */pnpm OR */bun))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/filev2\.getsession\.org$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|npx|yarn|pnpm|bun|curl|wget)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())

Shai-Hulud worm GitHub Action workflow file dropped under .github/workflows AIInstallation High
Detects file creation of shai-hulud-workflow.yml / shai-hulud.yaml / discussion.yaml under any .github/workflows/ directory on a developer host. The Shai-Hulud and Shai-Hulud 2.0 worms write this workflow then push it to a fresh branch so a PUSH-triggered Action exfiltrates harvested secrets. Rationale: Article references Mini Shai-Hulud and the postinstall credential-theft chain. Workflow filename triplet (shai-hulud-workflow.yml / shai-hulud.yaml / discussion.yaml) confirmed by Unit 42, Wiz, Datadog Security Labs and their public IOC repo. File-creation telemetry catches the worm during install-time, well before its GitHub push step. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://github.com/DataDog/indicators-of-compromise/tree/main/shai-hulud-2.0 • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546 T1567.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat researcher reproducing the worm in a contained lab repo
  • Red team / purple team retesting a previous Shai-Hulud incident
  • Backup software restoring an old repo snapshot that contained the file
  • Detection-engineering test ingesting public IOC samples
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sandbox","test-shai-hulud","ioc-repo") or DeviceName has_any ("sandbox-","detlab-","redteam-"))
Response runbook
Triage: dump the file SHA256 and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm parent is npm/yarn/pnpm/node and capture which package install triggered it. Pull the workflow YAML content to confirm it matches the worm template (push trigger + curl/base64 exfil block). Contain: kill the install process tree, delete the workflow file, revoke any GH PAT or npm token that the parent npm session had access to, and rotate cloud creds harvested by the worm payload. Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents on the same host for filev2.getsession.org or webhook.site over the past 24h; enumerate every other host that installed the same compromised package@version (npm cache, lockfile pushes); audit GitHub for any branch named shai-hulud-* or any new public repo named Shai-Hulud / matching 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming' description.
let WormFiles = dynamic(["shai-hulud-workflow.yml","shai-hulud.yaml","shai-hulud.yml","discussion.yaml","discussion.yml"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ (WormFiles)
| where FolderPath has @"\.github\workflows" or FolderPath has "/.github/workflows"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let WormFiles = dynamic(["shai-hulud-workflow.yml","shai-hulud.yaml","shai-hulud.yml","discussion.yaml","discussion.yml"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ (WormFiles)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\.github\workflows" or TargetFilePath has "/.github/workflows"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Shai-Hulud npm Worm GitHub Action Workflow File Written
id: 8a5d2b91-6c4f-4f17-9d83-2a7e8b9f4c12
description: Worm-signature workflow file written under .github/workflows/. The Shai-Hulud and Shai-Hulud 2.0 (Sha1-Hulud) self-replicating npm worms drop this and push to a fresh branch to exfiltrate harvested developer secrets via GitHub Actions.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
  - https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack
  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
  - https://github.com/DataDog/indicators-of-compromise/tree/main/shai-hulud-2.0
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1546
  - attack.t1567.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.github\workflows\'
      - '/.github/workflows/'
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\shai-hulud-workflow.yml'
      - '\shai-hulud.yaml'
      - '\shai-hulud.yml'
      - '\discussion.yaml'
      - '\discussion.yml'
      - '/shai-hulud-workflow.yml'
      - '/shai-hulud.yaml'
      - '/shai-hulud.yml'
      - '/discussion.yaml'
      - '/discussion.yml'
  condition: selection_path and selection_name
falsepositives:
  - Threat researcher reproducing the worm in a sandbox repo.
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\.github\\workflows\\shai-hulud-workflow.yml OR *\\.github\\workflows\\shai-hulud.yaml OR *\\.github\\workflows\\shai-hulud.yml OR *\\.github\\workflows\\discussion.yaml OR */\.github/workflows/shai-hulud-workflow.yml OR */\.github/workflows/shai-hulud.yaml OR */\.github/workflows/discussion.yaml))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(\\|\/)\.github(\\|\/)workflows(\\|\/)(shai-hulud-workflow\.yml|shai-hulud\.yaml|shai-hulud\.yml|discussion\.yaml|discussion\.yml)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","shai-hulud.yaml","shai-hulud.yml","discussion.yaml","discussion.yml") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.github\\workflows\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.github/workflows/*") by host Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

postmark-mcp BCC exfil to giftshop.club AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for outbound DNS/HTTPS to giftshop.club — the domain hosting phan@giftshop.club, the BCC recipient hard-coded into postmark-mcp v1.0.16 (the first publicly documented malicious npm-distributed MCP server, disclosed by Koi Security). Also catches BCC of organisational email to @giftshop.club via mail-flow telemetry. Rationale: Article lists giftshop.club in the IOC bundle. Koi Security (original disclosure), Snyk, BleepingComputer and the official Postmark advisory all confirm the BCC address phan@giftshop.club embedded in postmark-mcp v1.0.16. Detecting on the domain catches both the BCC mail leg (via Office mail-flow) and any local Node.js process resolving it during MCP server startup. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://postmarkapp.com/blog/information-regarding-malicious-postmark-mcp-package • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/first-malicious-mcp-server-found.html
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.003 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS Email.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Phishing-simulation vendor using lookalike domains for awareness training
  • Threat-intel feed validating the IOC with a passive DNS lookup
  • Security researcher resolving the domain from a sandbox
  • DLP egress test traffic targeting known-bad domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("smartscreen.exe","mpcmdrun.exe","defendersmartscreen.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: identify the AI assistant / MCP client invoking postmark-mcp (Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot Extensions) and the developer whose mailbox is integrated. Pull EmailEvents for the past 90 days to enumerate every message the MCP server sent and would have BCC'd. Contain: kill the MCP server process, uninstall postmark-mcp from every developer host (npm/pnpm/yarn ls -g and project node_modules), rotate the Postmark server token and any other credentials referenced in sent emails. Hunt: pivot on npm publisher 'phanpak' to identify the 31 other packages by the same author; query for any developer host that resolved giftshop.club or installed any package from publisher=phanpak in the last 6 months; review the affected mailbox for sensitive content the attacker now has copies of.
let IOC = dynamic(["giftshop.club"]);
let Net = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (IOC)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Actor=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Process=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Indicator=RemoteUrl, Path="network";
let Mail = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RecipientEmailAddress has_any (IOC) or SenderFromAddress has_any (IOC)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName="", Actor=SenderFromAddress, Process="", Cmd=Subject, Indicator=RecipientEmailAddress, Path="mail";
union Net, Mail
| order by Timestamp desc
let IOC = dynamic(["giftshop.club"]);
let Net = union isfuzzy=true
    (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any (IOC) | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Actor=SrcUsername, Indicator=DnsQuery, Path="dns"),
    (ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Url has_any (IOC) or DstHostname has_any (IOC) | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Actor=SrcUsername, Indicator=coalesce(Url,DstHostname), Path="web");
let Mail = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Operation in ("Send","SendOnBehalf","SendAs") and (Recipients has "giftshop.club" or P2RecipientList has "giftshop.club" or P2Sender has "giftshop.club")
    | project TimeGenerated, Host="", Actor=UserId, Indicator=tostring(Recipients), Path="mail";
union Net, Mail
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/yarn/pnpm postinstall hook spawning credential-harvest tooling AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for package-manager processes (npm/npx/yarn/pnpm/node/bun) spawning TruffleHog, curl/wget reaching the Shai-Hulud or postmark-mcp exfil hosts, or executing setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js — the signature install-time payload chain used by the Mini Shai-Hulud and Shai-Hulud 2.0 worms before EDR has a behavioural signal to bite on. Rationale: Article describes the npm postinstall credential-scraping chain (Mini Shai-Hulud, postmark-mcp). Datadog IOC repo, Wiz, Socket and Sysdig confirm setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js and TruffleHog binary execution from npm contexts as the post-compromise install-time signal — plus the webhook.site / filev2.getsession.org / giftshop.club exfil strings catch curl/wget invocations the worm chains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-strikes-again-tanstack-more-npm-packages-compromised • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://socket.dev/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/shai-hulud-the-novel-self-replicating-worm-infecting-hundreds-of-npm-packages • https://github.com/DataDog/indicators-of-compromise/tree/main/shai-hulud-2.0
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002 T1552.001 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD runners executing TruffleHog inside an npm script for legitimate secret scanning (e.g. GitHub Actions secret-scan job)
  • Developer using a Node-based wrapper around TruffleHog for repo audits
  • Build tooling that downloads bun via setup-bun in a controlled installer
  • Husky / lefthook pre-commit hooks running curl against internal services
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("buildkite-agent.exe","runner.exe","actions-runner.exe","jenkins.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("ci-","build-","runner-","github-actions-"))
Response runbook
Triage: capture full process tree (parent npm command → child) and the originating package name from npm's debug log (npm-debug.log / pnpm-debug.log / yarn-error.log). Confirm whether the executing npm install was kicked off by the developer or by a watch process. Contain: kill the install tree, roll back npm install in the project, and apply ignore-scripts=true in the user's .npmrc as a temporary hard-stop. Rotate any credentials the parent shell had in environment variables or files in ~/.config, ~/.aws, ~/.kube, ~/.npmrc, ~/.gitconfig. Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents on the host for filev2.getsession.org / giftshop.club / webhook.site / cyberhavenext.pro over the last 30 days; cross-ref every host that installed the same package@version from the lockfile diff; pivot on npm publisher to flag related malicious packages.
let PkgMgrs = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm.cmd","npx.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd","node.exe","bun.exe","npm","npx","node","yarn","pnpm","bun"]);
let SuspChildren = dynamic(["trufflehog.exe","trufflehog","curl.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe"]);
let SuspStrings = dynamic(["setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js","trufflehog","webhook.site","filev2.getsession.org","giftshop.club"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (PkgMgrs)
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (PkgMgrs)
| where FileName in~ (SuspChildren)
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspStrings)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspStrings)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let PkgMgrs = dynamic(["npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe","bun.exe","npm","npx","node","yarn","pnpm","bun"]);
let SuspChildren = dynamic(["trufflehog.exe","trufflehog","curl.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe"]);
let SuspStrings = dynamic(["setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js","trufflehog","webhook.site","filev2.getsession.org","giftshop.club"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any (PkgMgrs) or ActingProcessName has_any (PkgMgrs)
| where TargetProcessName has_any (SuspChildren) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspStrings) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspStrings)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Package-Manager Postinstall Hook Spawning Credential-Harvest Tooling
id: a1c7f4b3-8e6c-4f39-9a5b-4c9d0e1f6234
description: npm/npx/yarn/pnpm/node/bun spawning trufflehog, or executing setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js, or reaching Shai-Hulud / postmark-mcp exfil hosts — the install-time payload chain documented across the Mini Shai-Hulud and Shai-Hulud 2.0 npm worm waves.
references:
  - https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-strikes-again-tanstack-more-npm-packages-compromised
  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
  - https://socket.dev/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack
  - https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1195.002

logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  parent_pkg_mgr:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\npx.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '/npm'
      - '/npx'
      - '/node'
      - '/yarn'
      - '/pnpm'
      - '/bun'
  child_susp_tool:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\trufflehog.exe'
      - '\trufflehog'
      - '/trufflehog'
      - '\bun.exe'
  child_susp_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'setup_bun.js'
      - 'bun_environment.js'
      - 'trufflehog'
      - 'webhook.site'
      - 'filev2.getsession.org'
      - 'giftshop.club'

  - CI/CD pipelines that legitimately run trufflehog secret scanning inside npm scripts
  - Developers manually invoking trufflehog from a Node tool wrapper
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\npm.exe OR *\Npm.exe OR *\npx.exe OR *\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\yarn.exe OR *\pnpm.exe OR *\bun.exe) (@Image:(*\trufflehog.exe OR *\TruffleHog.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\wget.exe OR *\bun.exe) OR @CommandLine:(*setup_bun.js* OR *bun_environment.js* OR *trufflehog* OR *TruffleHog* OR *webhook.site* OR *filev2.getsession.org* OR *giftshop.club*))

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        Image|endswith:

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized axios npm package postinstall: node.exe spawned from plain-crypto-js dependency AIInstallation High
Hunts the postinstall hook of the malicious plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 dependency that ESET-mentioned trojanized axios versions (1.14.1, 0.30.4) silently pulled in. The malicious package's only purpose is to run `node setup.js` from its install folder, which then fetches a platform-specific RAT from C2. plain-crypto-js is never imported by axios source and is never a legitimate transitive dep. Rationale: plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 is the never-legitimate dependency injected by the trojanized axios versions; its postinstall fires `node setup.js`. Anchoring on the exact package name (case-sensitive on npm — always lowercase) gives near-zero FPs while catching every infected build host. Cross-checked against StepSecurity, Microsoft, Sophos, Datadog Security Labs and the axios GitHub post-mortem. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://github.com/axios/axios/issues/10636 • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the malicious package in a sandbox to write detections
  • SCA / dep-vuln scanner (Snyk, socket.dev, Mend) re-resolving lockfiles that still pin the bad version
  • Developer running `npm audit` against an old lockfile that lists plain-crypto-js
  • Mirror / proxy registry (Verdaccio, Nexus) replaying postinstalls during cache validation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\socket-cli\", @"\snyk\", @"\npm-audit\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm audit", "snyk test", "socket scan"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pivot to the host's package-manager footprint (npm/yarn/pnpm logs, .npm cache, project package-lock.json) and confirm axios was resolved at 1.14.1 or 0.30.4 around 2026-03-31 00:21–03:15 UTC. Identify the developer / build-pipeline identity that triggered the install. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, rotate all credentials, tokens and SSH/CI secrets that ever sat in env vars on it, kill any wt.exe / ld.py / com.apple.act.mond child processes, and force-pin axios to 1.14.0 / 0.30.3 across the org's lockfiles. Step 3 — Hunt: search all build agents and dev workstations for the C2 indicators (sfrclak.com, 142.11.206.73:8000) and for the persistence artifacts (UC2). Pull the host's outbound traffic for the 24h after install for staged credential exfil to packages.npm.org/product[012] paths.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where (FileName =~ "node.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "plain-crypto-js"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "plain-crypto-js"
   or FolderPath has @"\node_modules\plain-crypto-js\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "node.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "plain-crypto-js"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "plain-crypto-js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentName = ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildName = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 5c8b1f2a-7e4d-4d8a-9c2b-3f0a8e1b6d72

description: Detects node.exe execution referencing the malicious plain-crypto-js dependency injected by the trojanized axios versions 1.14.1 and 0.30.4 (npm supply chain compromise, 2026-03-31).

  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE) @CommandLine:*plain-crypto-js*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i CommandLine=/plain-crypto-js/i

axios RAT Windows persistence: %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe drop + %TEMP%\6202033.vbs/.ps1 staging AIInstallation High
Hunts the Windows-specific file artifacts dropped by the second-stage RAT delivered through the trojanized axios npm packages. The dropper writes %TEMP%\6202033.vbs and %TEMP%\6202033.ps1 as staging, then persists as %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe — note that legitimate Windows Terminal wt.exe lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps, NOT ProgramData, so the path itself is the discriminator. Rationale: Three high-specificity anchors from corroborated incident write-ups: %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe (Windows Terminal never installs there — it's in WindowsApps), %TEMP%\6202033.vbs and %TEMP%\6202033.ps1 (the C2 server id 6202033 is hard-coded in the dropper, so the filename literal is the IOC). The WindowsApps exclusion stops the only obvious FP path. Verified against StepSecurity, Datadog Security Labs, Sophos. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised-to-deploy-malware • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1059.001 T1059.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Store reinstalling Windows Terminal under a non-standard path on a heavily customised image
  • SCCM / Intune package that genuinely stages a renamed wt.exe in ProgramData (uncommon — verify owner)
  • Forensic tooling that copies artifacts into TEMP for analysis using a numeric ticket ID that happens to be 6202033
  • Backup or imaging product that round-trips the previously-dropped wt.exe out of quarantine
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("taskhostw.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","msiexec.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "userinit.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the writing process from InitiatingProcessFileName — expected chain is node.exe -> wscript.exe / powershell.exe writing the VBS/PS1, then VBS dropping wt.exe. Pull the SHA256 of wt.exe and submit to VT / Falcon Intelligence. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, kill the wt.exe and any persistence (Run keys, Scheduled Tasks, Services) pointing at it, quarantine all three files, rotate credentials of any user logged on during the install. Step 3 — Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents from the same host for connections to sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73:8000 (UC3); query the org for any other host that resolved sfrclak.com in the last 60 days even if no file artifact landed; review npm install history for axios 1.14.1 / 0.30.4.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FileName =~ "wt.exe" and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\" and not(FolderPath has @"\WindowsApps\"))
     or (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^6202033\.(vbs|ps1)$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFileName =~ "wt.exe" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\" and TargetFilePath !has @"\WindowsApps\")
     or (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^6202033\.(vbs|ps1)$")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: axios RAT artifacts - wt.exe in ProgramData or 6202033.vbs/.ps1 in TEMP
id: 9e2d4f81-3c6a-4f15-b8a3-2d7e9c4f1a55
status: experimental
description: Detects the Windows-stage file artifacts dropped by the trojanized axios npm packages (1.14.1 / 0.30.4 via plain-crypto-js@4.2.1). Real Windows Terminal wt.exe lives in WindowsApps, never ProgramData; the 6202033 numeric filename is the C2-server staging ID from the dropper.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/eset-apt-activity-report-q4-2025-q1-2026/
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan
  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.t1547.001
  - attack.t1036.005
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_wt:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\ProgramData\'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\wt.exe'
  selection_staging:
    TargetFilename|re: '(?i)\\Temp\\6202033\.(vbs|ps1)$'
  filter_winterminal:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\WindowsApps\'
  condition: (selection_wt or selection_staging) and not filter_winterminal
falsepositives:
  - In-house tooling that legitimately drops a wt.exe in ProgramData (rare — confirm with the owner)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\ProgramData\\wt.exe OR *\\programdata\\wt.exe) OR @TargetFilename:(*\\Temp\\6202033.vbs OR *\\Temp\\6202033.ps1 OR *\\TEMP\\6202033.vbs OR *\\TEMP\\6202033.ps1)) -@TargetFilename:*\\WindowsApps\\*
#event_simpleName=FileWritten (TargetFileName=/\\ProgramData\\wt\.exe$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\Temp\\6202033\.(vbs|ps1)$/i) NOT TargetFileName=/\\WindowsApps\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as process_name from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="wt.exe" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\wt.exe") OR Filesystem.file_name="6202033.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="6202033.ps1" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as process_name from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="wt.exe" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\wt.exe") OR Filesystem.file_name="6202033.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="6202033.ps1" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
axios RAT C2 callout to sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73:8000 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the dedicated C2 infrastructure of the second-stage RAT delivered via the trojanized axios npm packages. The dropper beacons to http://sfrclak.com:8000/6202033 to fetch platform-specific payloads, then POSTs back to packages.npm.org/product0|1|2 (note: the registry domain is spoofed in the URI path, the actual hostname is sfrclak.com). The IP 142.11.206.73 and port 8000 give a clean network-only fallback when DNS isn't logged. Rationale: sfrclak.com and 142.11.206.73:8000 are the dedicated, never-legitimate C2 for the axios RAT campaign — confirmed across StepSecurity, Microsoft, Sophos and Datadog Security Labs incident write-ups. Joining domain + IP + port covers the case where the host bypasses DNS (hard-coded IP) and where DNS is the only telemetry available. The 90-day lookback is intentional: the malicious packages were live only ~3 hours but compromised hosts may have beaconed since. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised-to-deploy-malware • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment platform (MISP, Recorded Future, internal TI scanner) probing the IOC
  • Security researcher reproducing the campaign in a lab segment
  • Web proxy / sandbox detonating sample URLs through corporate egress
  • DNS sinkhole that resolves but does not block — generates a query event with sinkhole RR data
  • WAF / SIEM enrichment job doing reverse-DNS lookups against the IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","curl.exe","misp-modules.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\TI-Enrichment\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull InitiatingProcessFileName for every beacon — legitimate beacons should be browsers from researchers; suspicious beacons will be node.exe, wscript.exe, powershell.exe, or %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe. Correlate the host to UC1/UC2 hits in the prior 24h. Step 2 — Contain: block sfrclak.com and 142.11.206.73 at the perimeter and DNS, isolate any matching host, rotate all secrets accessible from it. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessFolderPath for other node_modules paths to find sibling-compromised packages; query the entire fleet for resolutions of sfrclak.com going back 90 days; review egress proxy logs for POSTs to URI path patterns /product0, /product1, /product2 since those are the platform-tagged exfil endpoints even when the Host header is spoofed.
let C2Domain = dynamic(["sfrclak.com"]);
let C2IP = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2IP)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domain)
   or (RemoteIP in (C2IP) and RemotePort == 8000)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domain = dynamic(["sfrclak.com"]);
let C2IP = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where DstIpAddr in (C2IP) or DstHostname in~ (C2Domain) or Url has "sfrclak.com"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url, SrcUsername),
(ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where DnsQuery has "sfrclak.com"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: axios RAT C2 - sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73:8000
id: 7a1f3c8d-5b9e-4ea2-9f1c-8d3e7a2b6c44
status: experimental
description: Detects network communication with the dedicated C2 infrastructure of the second-stage RAT delivered via the trojanized axios npm packages (1.14.1, 0.30.4). C2 domain sfrclak.com resolves to 142.11.206.73, beacon endpoint /6202033 on TCP 8000.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/eset-apt-activity-report-q4-2025-q1-2026/
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_dns:
    QueryName|contains: 'sfrclak.com'
  condition: selection_dns
falsepositives:
  - Threat-intel enrichment services probing the IOC (CISA, abuse.ch, internal TI platform)
  - Security researcher reproducing the campaign
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationHostname:sfrclak.com OR @DestinationIp:142.11.206.73)) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:*sfrclak.com*)
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/sfrclak\.com$/i) OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="142.11.206.73" RemotePort=8000)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="sfrclak.com" OR DNS.query="*.sfrclak.com" by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | append [| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="142.11.206.73" AND All_Traffic.dest_port=8000 by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="sfrclak.com" OR DNS.query="*.sfrclak.com" by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="142.11.206.73" AND All_Traffic.dest_port=8000 by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`]
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
