Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/

tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm/pnpm install of trojanized codexui-android package on developer endpoint · [LLM] Android device installed gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app (mobile delivery of Codex token stealer)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Legitimate-Looking Codex Remote UI Secretly Steals Your AI Tokens
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS/HTTPS exfil to sentry.anyclaw.store (Codex token C2 masquerading as Sentry) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Codex-CLI node process reading ~/.codex/auth.json (Codex OAuth credential theft) · [LLM] HTTPS POST to /startlog with codexui User-Agent (Codex exfil over the wire) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
DNS/HTTPS exfil to sentry.anyclaw.store (Codex token C2 masquerading as Sentry) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution or outbound HTTPS to the attacker C2 anyclaw.store / sentry.anyclaw.store used by the trojanized codexui-android npm package and its companion Play Store apps to POST stolen Codex auth.json blobs to /startlog. Endpoint is deliberately named to blend with legitimate Sentry telemetry. Rationale: Domain sentry.anyclaw.store + path /startlog + User-Agent codexui/<ver> are unique strings from the article's exfil function. No legitimate use of anyclaw.store exists. Cross-checked: domain pattern matches Aikido's IOC publication and anyclaw.store appears as the only C2 host across both npm package and Android APK chains in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1036.005 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected - anyclaw.store is wholly attacker-controlled with no legitimate business use
  • Security researchers / IR teams sandboxing the malicious package
  • Threat-intel platforms enriching the domain via active resolution
  • Internal threat-hunting tooling deliberately probing the IOC
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the DeviceName/Computer + InitiatingProcessFileName for every hit; if InitiatingProcessFileName == node.exe or a node child of pnpm, treat as confirmed exfil. Pull DeviceFileEvents for ~/.codex/auth.json reads on the same host in the 5 min preceding the connection. 2. Contain: block anyclaw.store and *.anyclaw.store at the proxy / DNS sinkhole; isolate the affected developer endpoint; revoke and rotate the user's Codex/OpenAI session - force re-login from openai.com to invalidate stolen refresh_token; remove codexui-android from npm cache and node_modules. 3. Hunt: pivot to find every host that installed codexui-android@>=0.1.82 (look for pnpm/npm install events referencing the package), every Android device with gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app installed, and any other resolutions to *.anyclaw.store across the org.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("sentry.anyclaw.store","anyclaw.store") or RemoteUrl endswith ".anyclaw.store"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name endswith "anyclaw.store"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode),
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery endswith "anyclaw.store"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Name=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryTypeName, ResultCode=DnsResponseCodeName),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or RequestURL has "anyclaw.store/startlog" or RequestClientApplication startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Name=DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 1b3d6f2a-4a8e-4d9a-9c5b-7e2f8d1c4a01
description: Detects DNS or HTTP traffic to anyclaw.store / sentry.anyclaw.store used by the trojanized codexui-android npm package to exfiltrate Codex OAuth tokens.

npm/pnpm install of trojanized codexui-android package on developer endpoint AIDelivery High
Hunts the installation vector for the supply-chain attack - npm or pnpm pulling codexui-android (any version >= 0.1.82) onto a developer workstation or CI runner. The published npm artifact contains the malicious chunk-PUR7OUAG.js that the GitHub source does not. Rationale: `codexui-android` is the literal article-specific package name; chunk-PUR7OUAG.js is the unique malicious entry-point chunk only present in the npm artifact (never committed to GitHub). Either string in a node-tooling command line on a developer host is high-fidelity for this supply-chain attack. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-hunter intentionally pulling the package in an isolated VM
  • CI pipeline that legitimately depended on the package before disclosure (pre-2026-04 historical hits)
  • Reproduction of an Aikido write-up by a fellow detection engineer
  • Internal mirror/proxy syncing the package metadata
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the user is a developer; confirm whether the install completed (look for a follow-on DeviceFileEvents write of node_modules/codexui-android/dist-cli/index.js or chunk-PUR7OUAG.js). Check if the user has ever signed into Codex from this host (DeviceFileEvents for ~/.codex/auth.json). 2. Contain: remove the package (npm uninstall -g codexui-android, delete node_modules entry); block anyclaw.store at egress; force the user to revoke and re-issue their Codex/OpenAI session, treating refresh_token as compromised. 3. Hunt: enumerate every host that installed the package and any DeviceNetworkEvents to *.anyclaw.store from that host in the install window; look for the matching Android Play Store apps (gptos.intelligence.assistant, codex.app) on MDM-managed mobile devices.
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","node.exe") or FileName in~ ("npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe"))
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where FolderPath has "codexui-android" or FileName =~ "chunk-PUR7OUAG.js"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where (NewProcessName endswith "\\npm.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pnpm.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\yarn.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\npm.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\pnpm.exe")
    | where CommandLine has "codexui-android"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName),
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","pnpm","yarn","node") or ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","pnpm")
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, NewProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-Codex-CLI node process reading ~/.codex/auth.json (Codex OAuth credential theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access primitive of the codexui-android malware - a node process whose module path lives under codexui-android/dist-cli/ opening the Codex OAuth token store at ~/.codex/auth.json or $CODEX_HOME/auth.json. This catches the file-read step regardless of whether C2 succeeds. Rationale: The article's exfil function explicitly resolves $CODEX_HOME/auth.json and reads the whole file. Filename auth.json + parent dir .codex + reader process node (or anything in a codexui-android path) is a tight, article-specific triple. Filtering on InitiatingProcessFolderPath containing codexui-android removes legitimate Codex CLI use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate official Codex CLI reading its own auth.json during a normal user session
  • Developer running 'cat ~/.codex/auth.json' to debug their own token
  • Backup software enumerating the user's home directory
  • IDE plugin (e.g. official OpenAI VS Code extension) reading the token to authenticate
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "codexui-android" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("codexui-android","chunk-PUR7OUAG.js","dist-cli/index.js")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm InitiatingProcessFolderPath or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains codexui-android or chunk-PUR7OUAG.js - that disambiguates malicious from the legitimate Codex CLI. Correlate with DeviceNetworkEvents to anyclaw.store within +/-2 minutes. 2. Contain: kill the node process, isolate the host, revoke the user's Codex/OpenAI refresh_token via openai.com session management, and force re-authentication. Refresh tokens do not expire so revocation is critical. 3. Hunt: across the org, find every host that has ~/.codex/auth.json (DeviceFileEvents for the path) AND has installed codexui-android - those users' tokens must be treated as compromised since 0.1.82.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName == "auth.json"
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\.codex\\","/.codex/")

HTTPS POST to /startlog with codexui User-Agent (Codex exfil over the wire) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact exfil request shape - HTTPS POST to path /startlog with User-Agent matching ^codexui/<version>. Catches the malware even if the C2 domain is changed but URL/UA conventions remain. Targets proxy/firewall layer-7 telemetry. Rationale: Path /startlog and User-Agent prefix codexui/ are hard-coded in the article's httpsRequest options block. The UA prefix in particular is a self-identifying string the attacker chose - no legitimate Sentry SDK or anything else uses it. Catches mirror domains / IP fallbacks if the attacker rotates infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal app coincidentally exposing /startlog path (extremely unlikely; verify against asset inventory)
  • Security researcher posting deliberate test traffic to anyclaw.store
  • Honeypot / sinkhole infrastructure echoing the C2 path
  • Penetration test simulating the exact request shape
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull DeviceName/source-IP of the POST, identify the user, check if codexui-android is installed (npm ls / Android MDM inventory for gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app). 2. Contain: block sentry.anyclaw.store and *.anyclaw.store at egress; isolate the host; treat the user's Codex/OpenAI refresh_token as exfiltrated - revoke session via OpenAI account UI immediately (refresh tokens do not expire). 3. Hunt: search 60-day backwards for every POST to /startlog OR User-Agent starting with codexui/ across all proxy/firewall telemetry; pivot to every host that ever resolved anyclaw.store; review OpenAI/Codex audit logs for the affected user for anomalous source IPs or model invocations from unfamiliar geographies.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/startlog" or RemoteUrl has "anyclaw.store"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | where RequestURL has "/startlog" or DestinationHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or RequestClientApplication startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct),
  (ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
    | where Url has "/startlog" or HttpHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, RequestMethod=HttpMethod, RequestURL=Url, DestinationHostName=HttpHostName, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DeviceVendor=EventVendor, DeviceProduct=EventProduct),
  (W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where csMethod =~ "POST"
    | where csUriStem has "/startlog" or csUserAgent startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP=cIP, RequestMethod=csMethod, RequestURL=csUriStem, DestinationHostName=sSiteName, UserAgent=csUserAgent, DeviceVendor="Microsoft", DeviceProduct="IIS")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Android device installed gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app (mobile delivery of Codex token stealer) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the mobile delivery vector - Play Store installs of the BrutalStrike author's apps that bootstrap the malicious codexui-android npm package inside a PRoot Linux userland. Both APKs share the app.anyclaw.* Kotlin namespace and register the anyclaw://auth/codex-callback URI scheme. Rationale: Article-specific package IDs gptos.intelligence.assistant and codex.app are named explicitly as the two Play Store apps that bootstrap the malicious codexui-android npm package on first launch. Kotlin namespace app.anyclaw.* and URI scheme anyclaw://auth/codex-callback are shared signatures across both APKs and are not used by any legitimate app. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1474.003 T1456
Data sourcesEndpoint.Application_State
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately installed the app before disclosure (treat as compromised, not FP)
  • MDM test enrollment with the malicious APK as a test artifact
  • Mobile threat research team analysing the APK in a sandbox
  • Confusion with unrelated apps that happen to share the 'Codex' display name - validate on package id, not display name
Response runbook
1. Triage: list every Android device with gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app installed via MDM; identify if the user ever signed into Codex from the app (correlate with OpenAI audit logs for that user's account). 2. Contain: push an MDM uninstall policy for both package IDs; block sentry.anyclaw.store at corporate VPN / DNS egress; for every user who had the app, revoke their Codex/OpenAI session via openai.com - refresh tokens are non-expiring so they must be invalidated server-side. 3. Hunt: pivot to find every Codex API call to the user's account in the last 60 days from a source IP that doesn't match the user's typical geography/ASN; check whether the same publisher (BrutalStrike) has other apps in your org's MDM inventory (notably the Brutal Strike game with 5M+ installs).
DeviceInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where OSPlatform startswith "Android"
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where SoftwareName in~ ("gptos.intelligence.assistant","codex.app","OpenClaw Codex Claude AI Agent","Codex")
         or SoftwareVendor has "anyclaw"
  ) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OSPlatform startswith "Android"
| where SoftwareName in~ ("gptos.intelligence.assistant","codex.app","OpenClaw Codex Claude AI Agent","Codex")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by TimeGenerated desc
@mobile.app.package_name:(gptos.intelligence.assistant OR codex.app) OR @mobile.app.namespace:app.anyclaw.* OR @mobile.app.intent_filter.scheme:anyclaw
NETWORK
index=mdm OR index=intune (app_package_name="gptos.intelligence.assistant" OR app_package_name="codex.app" OR app_package="app.anyclaw.*" OR app_bundle_id="gptos.intelligence.assistant" OR app_bundle_id="codex.app") | stats earliest(_time) as firstSeen latest(_time) as lastSeen values(device_name) as device values(user) as user values(app_version) as version by app_package_name | convert ctime(firstSeen) ctime(lastSeen)

status: experimental
description: |

            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-48027 — Nx Console Embedded Malicious Code Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-05-27 5 use cases 3 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Nx Console contains an embedded malicious code vulnerability that allowed a malicious version of Nx Console to be published. The compromised extension fetched an obfuscated payload that could harvested credentials from multiple sources on disk and in memory. Vendor: Nx, Product: Nx Console. Known ransomware use: Known. Federal patch due: 2026-06-10.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

ImFileEvent

| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-8398")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-8398")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud 'gh-token-monitor' persistence daemon (LaunchAgent / systemd) · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm C2/exfil egress (masscan.cloud, git-tanstack.com, getsession.org) · [LLM] Package-manager process harvesting cloud metadata / Vault (IMDS 169.254.169.254, ECS 169.254.170.2, Vault :8200) · [LLM] npm/bun process writing GitHub Actions workflow files (worm secret-exfil injection) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm C2/exfil egress (masscan.cloud, git-tanstack.com, getsession.org) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound DNS/network connections to the Mini Shai-Hulud (TeamPCP) worm's confirmed exfiltration infrastructure used after a poisoned npm/PyPI package executes its install-time payload. These domains are credential dead-drops, not legitimate developer endpoints, so any resolution is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the article's extracted domains (api.masscan.cloud, git-tanstack.com, filev2/seed1.getsession.org) plus the corroborated zero.masscan.cloud:443/v1/telemetry exfil endpoint. StepSecurity/Wiz/OX/Splunk all confirm these as TeamPCP/Mini Shai-Hulud C2-dead-drop infra; VPC flow lacks domain names so cloudwatch is empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-strikes-again-tanstack-more-npm-packages-compromised • https://www.ox.security/blog/lightning-python-package-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/npm-supply-chain-attack-detection-analysis.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately running the Session messenger desktop client (resolves seed1/filev2.getsession.org) — verify the initiating process is a Session client, not node/npm
  • Security researcher detonating the malware in a sandbox that egresses to the lab's own DNS
  • Threat-intel enrichment/EDR sandbox sending these domains to a DNS sinkhole
  • Typosquat-monitoring tooling that proactively resolves git-tanstack.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("session.exe","session","session-desktop")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — if node/npm/npx/bun/python resolved the domain, treat as active compromise; pull the install log and recently modified package.json/package-lock.json. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke and rotate ALL developer credentials reachable from it (GitHub PAT, npm token, AWS keys, Vault tokens, SSH keys) since the worm harvests broadly. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for the gh-token-monitor persistence daemon, connections to 169.254.169.254/127.0.0.1:8200, and new/modified .github/workflows files; check npm/registry audit logs for any package published from this machine's tokens.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.masscan.cloud","zero.masscan.cloud","masscan.cloud","git-tanstack.com","filev2.getsession.org","seed1.getsession.org","getsession.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("masscan.cloud","git-tanstack.com","getsession.org")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Package-manager process harvesting cloud metadata / Vault (IMDS 169.254.169.254, ECS 169.254.170.2, Vault :8200) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts node/npm/npx/bun/yarn/pnpm or python reaching the AWS/ECS instance-metadata endpoints or a local HashiCorp Vault listener — the credential-harvesting step the Mini Shai-Hulud payload performs at install time. Package managers contacting link-local metadata IPs during dependency install is anomalous. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated network targets the StepSecurity write-up lists (169.254.169.254 IMDS, 169.254.170.2 ECS/Fargate creds, 127.0.0.1:8200 Vault) scoped to JS/Python package-manager parents, which is the worm's credential-access step. Sentinel ASIM network has no process field so this is best-effort and noisier there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://snyk.io/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1528
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node/Python application servers legitimately running on EC2/ECS that fetch IMDS via AWS SDK credential providers
  • CI runners that read instance role credentials at job start
  • Apps using Vault Agent on 127.0.0.1:8200 for secret injection
  • IMDSv2 token-fetch traffic from aws-sdk during normal operation
  • Container init scripts probing 169.254.170.2 for task role creds
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("prod","ci","runner","ecs","k8s")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is genuinely a server/CI runner (IMDS is normal there) vs a developer laptop (IMDS access is highly abnormal); inspect the parent command line for an in-progress `npm install`/`bun install`. 2) Contain: if a dev workstation, isolate and rotate any cloud role creds, Vault tokens, and registry tokens that the process could have read. 3) Hunt: correlate with egress to masscan.cloud/git-tanstack.com/getsession.org within the same session and check for the gh-token-monitor persistence daemon.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")) or (RemoteIP == "127.0.0.1" and RemotePort == 8200)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","node","npm","npm-cli.js","npx","bun.exe","bun","yarn","pnpm","python.exe","python","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")) or (DstIpAddr == "127.0.0.1" and DstPortNumber == 8200)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationIp:(169.254.169.254 OR 169.254.170.2) OR (@DestinationIp:127.0.0.1 AND @DestinationPort:8200)) @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\npm* OR *\npx* OR *\bun.exe OR *\Bun.exe OR *\yarn* OR *\pnpm* OR *\python.exe OR *\Python.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| (RemoteAddressIP4="169.254.169.254" OR RemoteAddressIP4="169.254.170.2" OR (RemoteAddressIP4="127.0.0.1" AND RemotePort=8200))
| ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|npx|bun|yarn|pnpm|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest IN ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2") OR (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" AND All_Traffic.dest_port=8200)) AND All_Traffic.app IN ("node","node.exe","npm","npx","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm","python","python3") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest IN ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2") OR (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" AND All_Traffic.dest_port=8200)) AND All_Traffic.app IN ("node","node.exe","npm","npx","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm","python","python3") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Mini Shai-Hulud 'gh-token-monitor' persistence daemon (LaunchAgent / systemd) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the worm's confirmed persistence component — a gh-token-monitor daemon installed as a macOS LaunchAgent or Linux systemd unit that polls GitHub every 60 seconds with stolen tokens. The filename string is a direct, high-fidelity IOC. Rationale: Direct match on the corroborated persistence-component name 'gh-token-monitor' and its LaunchAgent/systemd install locations from the StepSecurity attribution; the literal daemon name makes this near-zero-FP. Endpoint-only, so cloudwatch is empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/mini-shai-hulud-worm-compromises.html
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named internal automation script that happens to contain 'token-monitor' (verify exact 'gh-token-monitor' string)
  • Security tooling that creates honeyfiles with decoy names for canary detection
  • Developer-authored GitHub token-refresh helper installed as a LaunchAgent
  • Sandbox/IR replay of the malware sample writing the file
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the daemon's plist/unit file and the script it points at — confirm the 60-second GitHub polling loop and exfil URL; identify which user installed it and when. 2) Contain: unload/disable the LaunchAgent or systemd unit, delete the daemon, isolate the host, and immediately revoke the GitHub PAT(s) it polls with. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts with the same daemon, review GitHub audit log for token reuse from new IPs, and search egress logs for the masscan.cloud/getsession.org exfil domains from the same hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName has "gh-token-monitor"
   or (FolderPath has_any ("LaunchAgents","LaunchDaemons","/etc/systemd/system",".config/systemd") and FileName has "token")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName has "gh-token-monitor" or TargetFilePath has "gh-token-monitor"
   or (TargetFilePath has_any ("LaunchAgents","LaunchDaemons","/etc/systemd/system",".config/systemd") and TargetFileName has "token")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/bun process writing GitHub Actions workflow files (worm secret-exfil injection) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a JS package-manager process (node/npm/npx/bun/yarn/pnpm) creating or modifying files under .github/workflows — the Mini Shai-Hulud worm injects a malicious workflow that serializes repo secrets via toJSON(secrets) and posts them to api.masscan.cloud, enabling self-propagation through CI. Rationale: Targets the corroborated propagation mechanism (injected GitHub Actions workflow serializing toJSON(secrets) to api.masscan.cloud) by flagging package-manager processes writing workflow YAML — file content isn't in EDR file telemetry, so the parent-process + path combo is the pivot. Endpoint-only; cloudwatch empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://www.ox.security/blog/lightning-python-package-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack/ • https://about.gitlab.com/blog/gitlab-discovers-widespread-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project scaffolders/generators run via npx (e.g. create-react-app, nx, turbo) that legitimately write starter workflows
  • A developer running a codegen tool that templates CI workflows
  • Monorepo tooling (lerna/nx/turbo) regenerating workflow files
  • Dependabot/renovate local runs editing workflow pins
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("create-","generate","scaffold","nx ","turbo ","lerna ")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written workflow YAML and grep for `toJSON(secrets)`, `api.masscan.cloud`, curl/base64 exfil steps, or an unexpected `npm publish` step; confirm it wasn't a legitimate scaffolder by checking the parent command line. 2) Contain: if malicious, revert the workflow in the repo, isolate the host, rotate GitHub Actions secrets/OIDC and any registry publish tokens, and check whether the workflow already ran in CI. 3) Hunt: search the org's repos for the same injected workflow, review npm/PyPI for packages published from affected tokens, and correlate with masscan.cloud egress and the gh-token-monitor daemon on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has @"\.github\workflows" or FolderPath has "/.github/workflows")
| where FileName endswith ".yml" or FileName endswith ".yaml"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","node","npm","npm-cli.js","npx","bun.exe","bun","yarn","pnpm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\.github\workflows" or TargetFilePath has "/.github/workflows"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".yml" or TargetFileName endswith ".yaml"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","npx","bun","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1555.003

    category: file_access
    product: windows

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'

            - '\msedge.exe'

level: high

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - '\powershell.exe'

            - '\mshta.exe'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] BTMOB Android RAT APK SHA256 sighting in file or email telemetry · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BTMOB C2/phishing domain contact — arbsniper.com · [LLM] Egress to BTMOB hosted C2 cluster (LATAM/Hetzner IPs, Google CDN excluded) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
BTMOB C2/phishing domain contact — arbsniper.com AICommand & Control High
Detects any corporate-managed device (or perimeter proxy) resolving or connecting to arbsniper.com, the only non-CDN domain ESET ties to BTMOB Android RAT infrastructure. Catches infected BYOD on corporate WiFi, Windows endpoints that fetched the phishing lure, and proxy egress. Rationale: arbsniper.com is the single non-CDN C2/phishing domain ESET attributes to BTMOB and is also cited in Cyble's Feb 2025 write-up (https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/) and Malpedia (https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/apk.btmob). Two-source corroboration — high fidelity. The other ESET IPs include Google CDN ranges (74.125.x.x, 142.251.x.x, 173.194.x.x, 192.178.x.x) which would FP catastrophically; this UC pivots on the high-signal domain instead. Cross-checked against: • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/apk.btmob • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/btmob-android-rat-maas-builder/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / TI team manually browsing arbsniper.com from a corporate workstation for analysis
  • Automated sandbox/detonation traffic from an internal CAPE/CuckooFork host
  • DNS sinkhole that intentionally resolves the domain for logging
  • Internet-scanning project (Shodan-style) hitting the IP that happens to host the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("ti-analyst","sandbox-svc","detonation-svc") and DeviceName !startswith "SOC-LAB"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessFileName — if it's a browser, the user clicked a BTMOB lure; if it's a non-browser process (Java, Python, native PE) the host is likely already compromised and beaconing. Check user's recent email/SMS for BTMOB lures impersonating streaming, crypto-mining, or LATAM tax-authority brands (ESET cites Argentina ARCA). 2) Contain: block arbsniper.com at the proxy and DNS; if BYOD/MDM-enrolled, push device-quarantine / force MDM re-enrollment; revoke active SSO/VPN sessions for the user. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user across UrlClickEvents and EmailUrlInfo for related fake-store URLs; sweep DeviceFileEvents and EmailAttachmentInfo for the BTMOB APK SHA256 list (see sibling UC); enumerate other devices that resolved the domain in the last 30 days.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let BadDomain = "arbsniper.com";
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemoteUrl has BadDomain
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let BadDomain = "arbsniper.com";
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where Name has BadDomain
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", Host=Computer, ClientIP, Query=Name, Result=Result),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where RequestURL has BadDomain or DestinationHostName has BadDomain
  | project TimeGenerated, Source=DeviceVendor, Host=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Query=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName), Result=DeviceAction),
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where DnsQuery has BadDomain
  | project TimeGenerated, Source=EventProduct, Host=SrcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, Result=DnsResponseCodeName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects DNS resolution or network/web request to arbsniper.com, BTMOB Android RAT C2/phishing infrastructure tracked by ESET (April 2026) and Cyble (Feb 2025).
references:

(@network.destination.ip:* AND (@dns.question.name:*arbsniper.com OR @url:*arbsniper.com* OR @http.url:*arbsniper.com* OR @DestinationHostname:*arbsniper.com OR @QueryName:*arbsniper.com)) AND source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security OR zeek OR suricata OR proxy OR cloudflare OR cloudtrail)
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/arbsniper\.com$/i) OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|outlook|teams)\.exe$/i) | regex("arbsniper\.com", field=DomainName) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=[count(), min(@timestamp, as=firstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=lastSeen)])

BTMOB Android RAT APK SHA256 sighting in file or email telemetry AIDelivery Medium
Hash-IOC sweep for the BTMOB v2.5+ APK sample corpus published by ESET (cross-referenced with Cyble). Hits if any of the 36 SHA256s land on a managed endpoint via download, MDM sync staging directory, or arrive as an email attachment — covers the delivery stage for organisations with BYOD that touches corporate mail/file infra. Rationale: 36 SHA256 hashes published by ESET, with the family corroborated by Cyble (https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/), Malpedia (apk.btmob entry), and Infosecurity Magazine. Hash-IOC matches are unambiguous when they hit — main delivery vectors for corporate exposure are (a) APKs reaching mail attachments destined for company-issued Android devices, and (b) APKs landing in a Windows download folder before sideload to a paired Android device. Includes ImFileEvent for Sentinel cross-vendor portability. Cross-checked against: • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/apk.btmob • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/btmob-android-rat-maas-builder/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/btmob-android-rat-poses-significant-threat-with-easy-to-use-builder
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002 T1474.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Email.Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TI/RE analyst intentionally staging a known BTMOB sample on a sandbox host
  • AV/EDR signature-update package that ships hashes (rare — most vendors deliver hashes via signed catalog, not as raw files)
  • MDM / mobile-AV scanning hub that pulls APK samples for offline analysis
  • Penetration-testing lab building a knowledge base of public Android samples
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "SOC-LAB" and DeviceName !startswith "MALW-RE" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("sandbox-svc","ti-analyst","detonation-svc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm hostname is NOT in the TI/RE allowlist; pull FileOriginUrl and the email NetworkMessageId — if origin is a webmail attachment or fake-store URL, treat as live phishing. Identify the user and check for prior UrlClickEvents to BTMOB phishing themes (streaming, crypto-mining, LATAM tax/customs lures). 2) Contain: quarantine the file via Defender 'Stop and quarantine'; if the recipient is on managed Android, push MDM device-quarantine and revoke the user's SSO/MFA sessions; block the FileOriginUrl domain at proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot the SHA256 across the org via DeviceFileEvents/EmailAttachmentInfo for additional recipients; sweep network telemetry for arbsniper.com and the BTMOB hosted-IP cluster (see sibling UCs); check whether the user's Android device beaconed to those C2s in DeviceNetworkEvents from corporate WiFi.

Egress to BTMOB hosted C2 cluster (LATAM/Hetzner IPs, Google CDN excluded) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts corporate-network egress to the BTMOB C2 hosting footprint published by ESET, scoped to the non-CDN subset (Hetzner 178.156.x, LATAM bulletproof 191.96.x / 191.101.x / 200.9.x / 78.135.x / 79.133.x, Cloudflare front 104.21.64.137, 195.160.221.203). The Google IPs in ESET's IOC list are intentionally excluded because they are Google CDN ranges that would FP on every browser session. Rationale: Excludes the Google CDN ranges (74.125.x, 142.251.x, 173.194.x, 192.178.x) from ESET's IOC list which would generate overwhelming FPs on every browser session — these are Google services arbsniper.com / BTMOB happens to use for tracking/analytics, not C2. Focuses on the genuine BTMOB hosting footprint: Hetzner (178.156.x), LATAM bulletproof clusters (191.96.x, 191.101.x, 200.9.x), and the Cloudflare front (104.21.64.137). Hunting tier because the LATAM hosts may serve other tenants. Cyble's Feb 2025 write-up corroborates the LATAM C2 pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/apk.btmob
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate LATAM e-commerce / payments traffic to the 191.96.x.x bulletproof-hosting neighbour tenants (these IPs serve many low-reputation sites)
  • Cloudflare edge IP 104.21.64.137 being assigned to a benign customer domain after BTMOB rotated off — Cloudflare IPs are shared
  • Internet-scanning / threat-research traffic from a vuln-scanner that walks IP space
  • Travel-laptop user on LATAM hotel WiFi NATed through a shared address that happens to share a /24 with a flagged host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe") or RemotePort !in (80, 443) | where DeviceName !startswith "SOC-LAB" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("vuln-scanner","recon-svc")

1) Triage: enrich the RemoteIP with current passive DNS / Cloudflare reverse lookup — if PTR is now a clearly legitimate brand, downrate. For 104.21.64.137, check the HTTP Host header (proxy log) — if it's not arbsniper.com or an obvious lure domain, it's a Cloudflare neighbour and benign. 2) Contain: if the InitiatingProcessFileName is a corporate browser AND the connection went to the 191.96.x cluster, block the destination at the firewall and check the user for the BTMOB phishing lure in mail; if it's a non-browser process with no business case, isolate the host via Defender Live Response. 3) Hunt: pivot the user/host into the arbsniper.com UC and BTMOB APK SHA256 UC; check DeviceFileEvents for any newly-dropped APK or Android-emulator install (BlueStacks/NoxPlayer paired with these C2 calls would indicate desktop-side device-pairing test of a BTMOB build).
